title: Contarini and Cajetan: faith begins and ends in will; Bonaventure both powers
source_text: XXVIII. Huc spectant verba illa Cardinalis Contareni, in tractatu de Justificatione: Fides incipit a voluntate, quae obediens Deo & fidei, efficit ut intellectus assentiatur, absque haesitatione, traditis a Deo, & ideo promissionibus divinis confidat, & conceptat ex illis firmam fiduciam, quae pertinet ad voluntatem; ut quasi circulo quodam incipiat a voluntate haec fides, & desinat in voluntatem. Quibus consonat illud Cardinalis Cajetani, Credere in Deum est credendo confidere, & tendere in Deum, quod continet in se actum intellectus & voluntatis: in Joh. 6. Et eadem fuit sententia veterum Scholasticorum; qui teste Bonaventura in 3. Sent. dist. 23. docuerunt, fidem quodammodo esse in potentia cognitiva, & quodammodo in potentia affectiva; & ipse docet fidem, ut est virtus, & principium meriti, respicere liberum arbitrium, ut subjectum.
pass_a_gloss: Here belong those words of Cardinal Contarini in his treatise on Justification: Faith begins from the will, which, obedient to God and to faith, brings it about that the intellect assents without hesitation to things handed down by God, and therefore trusts the divine promises and conceives from them firm trust, which belongs to the will; so that as by a certain circle this faith begins from the will and ends in the will. With which agrees that of Cardinal Cajetan: To believe in God is by believing to trust and to tend into God, which contains in itself an act of intellect and of will (on John 6). And the same was the opinion of the older Scholastics; who, Bonaventure testifies on Sentences 3 dist. 23, taught that faith is somehow in the cognitive power and somehow in the affective power; and he himself teaches that faith, as it is a virtue and principle of merit, looks to free choice as subject.
pass_b_english: Contarini: faith begins in obedient will, yields intellect-assent and promise-trust, and ends again in will.
Cajetan (John 6) and Bonaventure: believing in God joins intellect and will / cognitive and affective powers.

choices.why: Subject of faith as virtue/merit for Bonaventure.
